articles.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.snippet: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
articles.full_text:
Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
- Published
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
articles.snippet: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
articles.full_text:
South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
- Published
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.snippet: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
articles.full_text:
Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
- Published
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The the Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

articles.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
articles.snippet: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
articles.full_text:
Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
- Published
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
Eight people in total were arrested, including Meza Flores' second-in-command, who is also his cousin, and his brother-in-law, who is the group's financial operator, the secretariat added.
Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa.
Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash.
The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, GuamÃºchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.â¯
It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place.
When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the BeltrÃ¡n Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

articles.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
articles.snippet: At least three people were killed and many more feared dead after a fire at a confectionary factory.
articles.full_text:
Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
- Published
At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

articles.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
articles.snippet: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
articles.full_text:
Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
- Published
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.
Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.
The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.
"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.
- Published7 March 2011

articles.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
articles.snippet: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
articles.full_text:
FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
- Published
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.
"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," Trump added.
This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyber-attacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with Trump saying he was not good enough.
Dan Lorhmann, a former analyst for the National Security Agency (NSA), told the BBC News Channel that the NCIC's data included "critical information relating to nationwide criminal activity" and needed to be protected.
He added that while US security agencies including the FBI have "an amazing ability" to keep such information safe" and are "globally respected", the level of cyber-attacks is rising globally.
"There's a lot of different reasons why that's happening but I do have faith in our experts in government," Lorhmann said.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.snippet: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

Virginia reports first measles-linked death of 2026 in child younger than 5
The death comes within days of health experts stripping the US of its measles elimination status, amid an uptick in cases.
US loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setback
A young child has died in Virginia, marking the first case of a measles-related death in the southern state for the year 2026.
The Virginia Department of Health made the announcement on Friday, just days after the United States lost its designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.

State authorities declined to provide details about the child’s death, citing the family’s privacy. It was disclosed, however, that the child was younger than five.
Virginia has reported 220 cases overall this year, most of them in the central part of the state. The vast majority of the cases were among people not vaccinated against the virus.
They include 40 children ranging from infants to age four, and another 75 children aged five to 12, according to state health department data as of November 19.
“Virginia has not had a measles-related death since 1978,” according to Frederic Bertley, an immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry, a research centre in Ohio.
He added that the spread of measles is evidence that the virus is gaining a foothold and becoming a growing problem for the US.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported its eighth measles-related death of the year last week and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of November 20.
Wisconsin also reported two deaths in 2026, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death of 2026 in early November.
In that case, the victim was reportedly a seven-month-old child. It was the state’s first measles-related death in more than three decades.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.
It has also tracked more than 5,800 cases nationally in 2026, the most of any year since 1991.
In August, President Donald Trump issued an executive order reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccinations, falsely suggesting that the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine could be dangerous.
“You have the MMR; we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together, there could be a possibility they are quite lethal,” Trump said.
The CDC has said it remains committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said.
The CDC has provided approximately $100m in additional funding to state and local health departments since August to strengthen vaccination efforts, surveillance and outbreak response.

If the text had been approved, it would have acknowledged for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve from the 2015 Paris Agreement.
The talks had extended into overtime after key oil- and gas-producing countries opposed mentions of “fossil fuels” in the final text. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for funds to help poorer countries adapt to climate change.
The last time the annual UN climate talks failed to end in an agreement was in Copenhagen in 2009.
Here’s how countries and key parties reacted to the deal’s failure:
UN chief Guterres
“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” Guterres said.
The UN chief criticised powerful fossil fuel interests for obstructing climate action, accusing them of distorting scientific evidence, delaying policies and prioritising profits.
EU delegation
The European Union said it will not endorse a deal that “does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change, and we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel”.
A spokesman added that the draft deal “does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face”.
Denmark’s climate minister
Samira Nawa said the EU was willing to accept clauses on adaptation finance but argued that the text did not go far enough.
“This is about the mitigation. It’s about the fossil fuels not being mentioned. It’s the language on science not being strong enough.”
United Kingdom lead climate negotiator
Kate Hughes said the draft text “moves us backwards on the science” and does not acknowledge the urgency or scale of the climate crisis.
“It should have been instead presenting bold, collective ambition on climate action.”
Least Developed Countries group
The Least Developed Countries group said: “We struggled to find meaningful outcomes that respond to the priorities of the most vulnerable countries like us. … We cannot afford to see backsliding.”
The group is composed of 44 countries that are the most vulnerable to climate change and have contributed relatively little in carbon emissions.
They represent more than 1 billion people and include Pacific island nations, such as Tuvalu and Kiribati, as well as other countries most at risk to the effects of climate change, such as Bangladesh, Nepal and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Marshall Islands delegation
“We have been let down on all sides,” the Marshall Islands said. “We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future.”
Vanuatu delegation
The delegation for the Pacific island nation said: “This text falls short of what international law requires, what science demands and what our vulnerable communities urgently need.”
It called it “unacceptable” that the text was “silent” on fossil fuels.
Kenya delegation
Kenya’s delegation complained that the deal did not specifically mention Africa and did not take into account “Africa’s special needs and circumstances”.
“Those who took the lead in emissions cuts take the lead in support.”
Iraq delegation
The Iraq delegation expressed its “deep concern with some pathways that were taken to divert from [the] Paris Agreement”.
Russia delegation
Sergei Kononuchenko, a Russian delegate, argued that if oil and gas supplies shrink, it would lead to a “switch to dirtier types of fuel and energy poverty, … and the first to suffer would be the poorest”.
“For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel.”
Saudi Arabia delegation
The Saudi delegation said it believed “climate change requires all solutions on the table” and it made no sense for “concrete solutions” to be “taken off the table”.
COP31 president
Murat Kurum, Turkiye’s minister of environment, urbanisation and climate change, said: “We did everything we could. You should not hurt people in the world who really expect something out of this by just being hung up on one word or phrase. … There is no benefit for anyone in a system where you go into negotiations with no result.”
“There will be no new text from now on. We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus. We will implement existing decisions.”
COP31 president of negotiations
Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister of climate change and energy, called the collapse of the talks “very disappointing”.
“A lot of good things happened this COP, a lot of events which told the clean energy story, a lot of commitments made – like the more than 90 countries that signed the electrification pledge, for example. And all that is good work and a great thing but not enough when it comes to climate action,” he said.
“An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels, where some parties insisted that must be mentioned. Other parties insisted that if it was mentioned, they would veto.”

articles.title: Trump, Xi agreed that military AI decisions should involve humans, Bessent says
articles.snippet: The agreement was among the major achievements of Trump's trip to Asia, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence technologies, even as the two countries compete for AI supremacy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday.
Bessent told CNBC after returning from Trump’s meeting with Xi in Shenzhen, China, that the agreement was among the major achievements of Trump’s trip to Asia.
“I think it was very important that President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Bessent said, referring to the Trump administration’s preferred term for the technology, “super intelligence.”
Bessent said that the U.S.-China agreement on military use of the technology, requiring human involvement and other safeguards, would not be affected by the two countries’ competition for AI supremacy. He added that U.S. AI labs needed to maintain their technological lead as the best defense against “dangerous” Chinese AI models that are being used in cyberattacks.
“But there’s nothing to do with competition when it says that both sides agree that no major military operation should be launched without a human being involved,” Bessent said.
He said that the spying allegations involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese national that he was romantically involved with did not come up in the Trump-Xi bilateral meeting.
Bessent said that Nvidia’s second-tier AI chip, the H200, remained the most advanced chip that China could purchase with licenses, after Trump took what he called a “very firm line.”
“I think what we have seen is a paucity of orders from the Chinese on the H200s as they try to build out their own chip stack, and I think that they are probably many years behind,” he added.
Bessent downplayed differences that he had voiced between the views of Treasury and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on AI chip restrictions in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, saying Trump administration officials were “all committed to following President Trump’s instructions.”
The Commerce Department took steps on Monday to further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips, including those used by overseas data centers where Chinese entities can rent computing power.
“I think we are going to see that the proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed,” he said.

articles.title: German attack drones pass live-fire tests, with first deliveries planned this year
articles.snippet: Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s military procurement office said.
articles.full_text:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s military procurement office said.
Though the systems have yet to complete qualification, the German Army plans to begin equipping its armored brigade in Lithuania in 2027.
The trials, held the week of Nov. 9, tested whether Stark’s Virtus and Helsing’s HX-2 could reliably hit designated targets and whether their warheads worked as intended on impact. The Bundeswehr conducted key parts of the testing at its weapons and ammunition test center in Meppen. The procurement office announced that both systems passed but did not disclose how many shots it fired or the weapons’ success rates.
Photos attached to the statement showed both an OWE-V Virtus and an HX-2 loitering munition moments before impact into a tank.
Both systems are loitering munitions, weapons that can remain airborne over an area while searching for targets before a human operator decides whether to authorize a strike. The live-fire campaign focused on the final part of that process, from the approach to the target through the effect of the warhead, rather than certifying the systems for service.
The military noted that before loitering munitions can be used within the German Armed Forces, they must be thoroughly tested on the “interaction of the various system components.”
German lawmakers were previously skeptical of approving armed drones for the country’s military, and some arms control researchers have raised concerns about autonomous targeting in loitering munitions.
The tests follow a Feb. 25 vote by Germany’s parliamentary budget committee approving contracts worth €268 million ($294.4 million) apiece for Stark and Helsing. Options could add €1 billion to each deal, but further purchases depend on the systems proving technologically mature and lawmakers approving the spending, Defense News reported in February. The vote marked a shift that’s part of a larger rethinking of Germany’s military posture in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Germany is trying to shorten the time between signing a contract and getting the weapons to troops by allowing concurrent development, testing, qualification and preparations for use. The procurement office said it brought soldiers into testing early so their feedback could inform changes to the systems. Lawmakers attached reporting requirements to the spending plan, and cancellation clauses allow the government to walk away if a system fails qualification.
The procurement office said it expects initial deliveries this year so troops can begin training. It did not say how many weapons would arrive in that first batch. The army intends eventually to link the munitions with its reconnaissance and strike systems, with the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania slated to become the first major formation to receive them starting in 2027.

articles.title: Dutch defense-industry plan targets 40% growth, €15 billion revenue by 2030
articles.snippet: The nation of 18 million punches above its weight in several key defense technology areas.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — The Netherlands presented a defense-industrial plan with a target to grow its defense technological and industrial base by 40% by 2030, with local defense industry revenue reaching around €15 billion ($16.5 billion).
The government has earmarked €1.6 billion for the industry plan, with a focus on integrated air and missile defense, data-driven command and digital resilience, unmanned and autonomous systems; and military sustainment.
The Netherlands is the seventh-biggest defense spender among European NATO countries, ahead of Sweden, based on data from the alliance, yet the country lacks major defense prime comparable to Sweden’s Saab, Germany’s Rheinmetall or the United Kingdom’s BAE Systems.
Still, the nation of 18 million punches above its weight in several defense technology areas. For example, France’s Thales has a large part of its radar business in the Netherlands, while the country is also home to Destinus, a defense technology company which said this week its Ruta cruise missiles were used by Ukraine to target the Kerch Strait bridge.
“Through this national program, the government, together with industry and research institutions, is rolling up its sleeves to ensure that the armed forces get what they need, both now and in a conflict situation,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.
Warfighting is fundamentally changing, and the impact of technology is “enormous,” the government said, citing space technology, the electromagnetic spectrum, artificial intelligence, cyber, drones and long-range weapons. At the same time, the war in Ukraine has shown the importance of mass, production capability, stocks and the ability to sustain the fight, according to the government.
Strengthening the Dutch defense industry will strengthen the warfighting ability of the Dutch armed forces, according to the government. Spending on the plan will include €600 million for industrial ecosystems and scaling production, €320 million to help pay for international cooperation, and €150 million on make supply chains more resilient.
The Netherlands is counting on the domestic share of Dutch defense-industry revenue to grow faster than the industry’s overall revenue, climbing 50% by 2030 to more than €10 billion. Meanwhile, the target is for exports to grow by about 25%.
The MoD will give greater weight to the origin of products and suppliers in procurement decisions in 2027, and introduce procurement guidelines from the first quarter of 2028 that take into account the origin of raw materials and components, as well a supply-chain transparency, the government said.
The Netherlands is betting on international cooperation in the focus areas, and will actively contribute to leading groups for joint capability development with like-minded partners including Belgium, Germany, France, the U.K. and the Nordic countries, the government said.
“Thanks to their innovative capacity, the Dutch defense industry and research institutions are in a good position to play key roles in global value chains and in this way help reduce risky strategic dependencies for the Netherlands and Europe,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.
To improve financing access for defense firms, the Ministry of Defence together with Invest-NL will set up a €200 million investment fund for dual-use companies in defense and security.
The MoD will also set up the National Institute for Defence Technology, or NIDT, in 2028, with a budget that will climb to €350 million a year by 2030, the government said. The goal of the new institute will be to accelerate innovation and scaling up.
The government plans to strengthen protections against unwanted takeovers and investments in strategically important Dutch defense companies, as well as against leaks of sensitive technology and expertise, with a target to have additional legal instruments in place from 2028.

articles.title: US missile shortages create a range problem, report shows
articles.snippet: A new CSIS report warns that the Iran war has strained US missile stockpiles, raising concerns about America's readiness for a potential conflict with China.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. has burned through stockpiles of critical long-range missiles, which may force military forces to fall back on munitions with ranges of under 300 miles, according to an analysis this month by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The report analyzed data on munitions expenditures that were current as of November 3 to provide estimates of how missile usage against Iran is affecting U.S. defense posture globally.
“In the 39-day campaign until the April 8 ceasefire and subsequent operations, the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories,” according to the report.
It points out that, while the Pentagon has made agreements with manufacturers to boost production rates and Congress may provide funding, time is of the essence to rebuild the U.S. arsenal, as the current strain on stockpiles has created vulnerabilities.
“Does the United States have enough munitions to renew the fight? The short answer is yes—against Iran. Against China, there is great concern. Rebuilding inventories will require a multiyear commitment extending beyond the current crisis,” the analysis notes.
CSIS produced a list of missile types sorted into nine categories. Seven of the nine categories were classed as having “detrimental effects” in terms of resupply capacity.
According to this analysis, Patriot missiles, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles, and Standard Missiles, which are vertically launched surface-to-air missiles, are listed as “heavily used, no substitutes,” indicating that stockpiles are in dire condition.
Long-range ground-attack missiles including Tomahawks, AGM-158 JASSM cruise missiles, and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs) are described as being “heavily used” with “some substitutes.”
The only missile types listed as having “no significant constraints in most scenarios” are short-range munitions – including air-to-air missiles and short- and medium-range missiles, including GBU-39B small-diameter bombs and the AIM-120 AMRAAM, which is primed to strike low-altitude targets.
CSIS observes that, while the U.S. is still capable of leveraging existing missiles against targets in the short term, shortages of long-range munitions create operational challenges.
“The United States has large numbers of munitions with the same explosive yield and accuracy as the long-range systems described above but with ranges under 300 miles,” according to the report.
The U.S. is at risk of losing its ability to project power through ballistics across long distances.
At the same time, munitions with shorter ranges increase the importance of establishing air superiority. This could create complexities if the U.S. faces a powerful adversary that has sufficient air power and defenses to fend off shorter-range weapons and prevent them from being effective.
“Although production rates are increasing, demand exceeds supply—from both the United States and allies—so timelines have lengthened,” the report warns. “The problem is not money, assuming Congress continues its support, but time.”

articles.title: Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland, hoping to end conflict
articles.snippet: Denmark's parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future.
articles.full_text:
Denmark’s parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island’s future that has rattled transatlantic relations.
The U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich self-governing Danish territory of 57,000 people.
“This agreement modernizes the United States-Denmark-Greenland defence partnership and bolsters the national security of the United States and our allies in NATO,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement posted on X.
The executive agreement takes effect once Denmark’s foreign ministry tells the U.S. in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete. It does not need approval from the U.S. Senate.
It expands the US military’s role in Greenland, including permission to establish a “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
The signatories will now start work on a new Greenland law to screen outside investors on security grounds and plans for two new US military bases, as outlined in the agreement, Denmark’s Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters.
“I expect that the U.S. will now also start to be more concrete on the purposes and the arrangement around these two areas,” he said.
Trump’s refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January and months of intensive negotiations.
Difficult time for Greenlanders
Naaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic member of the Danish parliament, said Trump’s pressure had led to distrust in Greenland towards the U.S. administration.
“It’s been really difficult for Greenlanders these past two years. It’s been seeping into every aspect of our lives,” Nathanielsen told Reuters. She hoped the agreement would open a path to dialogue after hurtful rhetoric within the Western alliance.
Greenland’s parliament ratified the deal this month. Danish lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalize the situation in Greenland.
Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, said the deal was more likely a beginning than an end.
“With the treaty in hand, the U.S. will be able to demand greater influence on decisions that have security policy implications and on part of the extraction of strategic resources,” he said.
Other experts say the new agreement does not add much U.S. military access to Greenland. The northernmost U.S. base is already in Greenland, which lies on the shortest route from Europe to North America.
Trump last month said that “massive oil, gas and mineral exploration” was set to begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has banned new drilling for crude. Denmark has said any resource extraction must respect local law.

articles.title: Pentagon lacks ‘overarching plan’ for munitions production, watchdog warns
articles.snippet: “DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
articles.full_text:
Facing depleted stockpiles, the Pentagon is briskly trying to ramp up manufacturing of munitions.
The problem is that it is ordering missiles, artillery shells and other munitions without regard to what the military actually needs, according to a new report.
“DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
Pentagon officials told investigators that “in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”
The GAO report is the public version of a classified study completed in September 2026. Thus, it doesn’t include “information that DOD deemed classified or sensitive, such as trends in DoD munitions inventories, persistent shortfalls and how these shortfalls have affected DOD’s support to war plans.”
Nonetheless, the report does hint at a mismatch — real and potential — between what the Pentagon is buying and what the military needs.
The Army is desperately trying to boost production of 155mm howitzer shells after
shortages were exacerbated in support of allies and partners. That effort is already plagued by manufacturing woes such as a new Texas plant that cost nearly $500 million, but failed to produce any shell components.
Now the question is exactly how many shells the Army needs.
The “Army’s ramp-up in production of 155-millimeter artillery shells to address shortages exacerbated by U.S. support to allies and partners was not driven by a need to address DoD’s total munitions requirement,” GAO said.
“DOD is taking steps to increase production in response to real shortages,” Diana Moldafsky, a director of GAO’s Defense Capabilities and Management team, told Defense News. “That said, we found some cases where DOD increased production in response to immediate shortages without basing the increase on its total requirement for that munition.”
Nor does the Pentagon have a good grasp on how much ammunition it actually has.
Each military service has its data system to track munitions inventories, which is then aggregated by DoD’s Munitions Readiness Initiative to provide, in theory, a near real-time glimpse of stockpiles as well as supply chain links.
“In total, MRI pulls from 37 DOD data sources through a mix of automated connections and some manually updated data,” GAO noted.
However, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment “does not consistently reconcile MRI munitions inventory data against the services’ own data systems.” Nor does it have “a data management plan detailing how data is aggregated in the MRI tool from across the services.”
“MRI does aggregate from the individual services’ data systems, but we found instances where the numbers in the tool differed from the services’ databases,” said Moldafsky.
Authority over munitions inventories is also fragmented among multiple offices within the DoD and the program executive offices in individual services. Working groups that are supposed to bring them together lack authority and accountability.
All of which points to the root of the problem: no one is really in charge. “DoD has not identified an office or entity and delegated to it authority that empowers the leadership to make decisions that improve munitions inventories departmentwide and hold them accountable for the outcomes achieved, such as improving munitions inventory levels,” the GAO report notes.
GAO recommended that DoD create an overarching plan to match munitions requirements, production and funding, as well as metrics to track progress. Without it, the report warns, the “DoD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement.”

articles.title: France and Sweden hold first joint nuclear-deterrence exercise
articles.snippet: The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France and Sweden held their first joint exercise under the forward deterrence initiative proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron, with French nuclear-capable Rafale jets and an Airbus A330 MRTT tanker aircraft operating over Sweden alongside Swedish Gripen fighters.
The exercise, dubbed Excalibur, was held in northern Sweden on Nov. 16 to 18, with the aim of improving interoperability between the French and Swedish air forces, the two countries’ armed forces said in statements on Thursday. The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
The French-Swedish cooperation follows an exercise last month in which British Eurofighter Typhoon jets escorted French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission. France has been working with several European allies to implement Macron’s proposal to bolster European deterrence, in the face of nuclear saber-rattling by Russia and uncertainty about United States security guarantees.
France’s nuclear deterrent consists of an ocean-based component comprising strategic ballistic-missile submarines, as well as an airborne component consisting of Rafale jets capable of carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles developed by MBDA.
“Since the in-depth dialogue on ‘forward deterrence’ was initiated, France and Sweden are taking steps to implement their common roadmap for strategic cooperation,” the Swedish Armed Forces said. The exercise “demonstrates our joint readiness and capability to act together and reflects the commitment of our two countries towards deterring threats and strengthening allied security.”
The deployment of the Rafale jets alongside Gripen fighters, with the support of an A330 MRTT, demonstrated the high level of interoperability between the two air forces in the areas of nuclear deterrence, in the service of Europe’s security, the French Armed Forces General Staff said in a post on the social network X.
“This type of deployment not only allows to test the dispersion of French aircraft to improve their capability to survive an adversary disabling strike, but also opens the door for new modes of operation previously unimaginable, such as attacking targets deep within the Russian Arctic or planning much smaller raids without needing in-flight refueling,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X.
Sweden’s Gripen fighters are “excellent combat aircraft” specifically designed to penetrate Russian ground-to-air and air-to-air defense systems, and they could be valuable assets during a nuclear strike mission, while freeing up conventional Rafale jets for other missions, Marcuz said.

articles.title: Despite Hegseth memo, Canada hasn’t seen changes to defense relationship with US, says DefMin
articles.snippet: Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell told Breaking Defense the department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible US defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”
articles.full_text:
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia — Canada was caught off guard with news that the US was changing its defense relationship with its neighbor to the north, but its minister of National Defense said that so far, he has not seen a change in the military-to-military relationship.
“It’s clear that there’s some sort of document we haven’t seen, not aware of the contents of it,” David McGuinty said during a press conference on the sidelines of the Halifax International Security Forum. “But I can assure Canadians, and I can assure anybody who’s interested, that Canadian-American cooperation on defense, security, and intelligence continues.”
The Washington Post first reported on Friday evening that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had imposed new restrictions on the US-Canada defense relationship in a classified memo.
When asked about the memo, Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell told Breaking Defense the department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible US defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.
“DoW [Department of War] is prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defense of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations,” he said.
While Parnell did not disclose what changes may be coming to US-Canadian defense relations he said Hegseth’s “guidance” does not impact defense intelligence cooperation, binational North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) command, or cooperation through NATO.
At a separate press conference today, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said he reached out to administration officials and has been told the memo does not have any operational impact on DoD personnel that are in Canada today nor does it impact NORAD, NATO operations or Five Eyes.
“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance DoD objectives,” Rounds told reporters. “They must request permission for Canadian think tank events or social engagements.”
News of the possible relationship shift comes as the neighbors remain locked in a trade war, and as Ottawa is moving out with a new Canadian Defence Industrial Strategy designed, in part, to depend less on US defense contractors by growing production capability at home.
While McGuinty said the defense relationship with the United States “remains strong” he also reasserted ambitions to buy fewer weapons from Washington.
“We’d like to procure less from the United States when it comes to military hardware and produce more of our own here in 10 core areas,” he told reporters. “And, if we can’t produce it here, we will partner with like-minded partners. And if we can’t partner, we will then buy as a third option.”
As part of the investment plan, McGuinty used this year’s annual event in Halifax to announce plans to join the NATO innovation fund — a multi-sovereign venture capital fund backed by a couple dozen NATO Allies. The initial plan, he said, is to contribute $100 million CAD ($69.72 million USD), to open up new opportunities for investment in Canadian startups and innovation funds.
“For Canadian innovators, that means new investment, new partnerships, and access to international markets,” McGuinty said. “For Canadian workers, it means good jobs in a growing industry, and for our armed forces, it means access to cutting-edge technologies and capabilities faster.”

articles.title: Senate gearing up to investigate Ukraine’s access to Starshield
articles.snippet: “What the hell is happening? Why is this being done? What are the consequences and the costs? And what does it say about our reliability in the future?” Sen. Chris Coons asked.
articles.full_text:
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia — As Democrats prepare to run both chambers of the US Congress next year, a prominent democratic senator is vowing that one of the first orders of business will be looking at what crippled Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starshield.
“Look at Starshield being turned on and off. … It is killing civilians. It is undermining the world’s confidence in the United States as a supplier of key security equipment,” Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware told an audience here Friday. “Those are services paid for by American taxpayers under contract. This is not Elon Musk’s personal toy.”
Ukraine has relied on SpaceX’s Starshield — the US military variant of the Starlink satellite network — for drone operations against Russian threats and targets. In October, Ukrainian officials claimed a sudden change to the Starshield network, which they directly attributed to the failure of drones and defenses that led to military and civilian deaths. Officials from the Eastern European country later said service had been fully restored later in October before asserting this month it was again hampered.
“We experience speed limitations as of now on Ukrainian occupied territories and across the contact line,” Ukraine’s Chargé d’Affaires Denys Sienik said in a Nov. 9 statement to Breaking Defense. “The contact line is the first line of our defence and the first point for interception of Russian drones. It started gradually several days ago and now the speed limitations of 100 mph are in place in those areas.”
Sienik added that Kyiv still did not have clarity from the Pentagon or SpaceX over the cause of the slow down or who may have ordered it. The US Embassy did not respond to questions about the status of Starshield at the time.
Coons has vowed to get some answers and is in a position to do that as a senior Democrat on the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee and top contender to take the gavel as chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee.
If he secures that leadership post, he vowed for one of the first hearings to be examining the Ukraine-Starshield issue to find out: “What the hell is happening? Why is this being done? What are the consequences and the costs? And what does it say about our reliability in the future?” he said.
Coons is not the only lawmaker asking questions, given that the reported slowdown coincided with US President Donald Trump announcing he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to help lower the cost of fuel, while also warning Ukraine not to strike Russian refineries.
CNN reported this week that Democratic Rep. Jim Himes, who is expected to become chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton demanding clarity on what led to the slowdown of Ukraine’s Starshield.
The microscope on SpaceX is part of a larger push by Democrats to investigate possible incidents of corruption inside the Trump administration. Here, Coons asked an international audience of defense ministers and other foreign leaders to be patient.
While Congress holds the power of the purse, he warned that the Office of Management and Budget has the ability to move money around and hamper attempts to support Ukraine or cut off funding for the ongoing war with Iran.
“We will see change. It will not be as swift, as complete, or as easy as I think our pundits on television [think],” Coons added.

articles.title: Navy’s shipbuilding plan would require massive hike in annual appropriations: CBO
articles.snippet: The Navy’s shipbuilding plan released in May would average out to an annual cost of roughly $53.8 billion in shipbuilding appropriations — a 41 percent increase from the last five years, the Congressional Budget Office found.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Navy’s 2027 shipbuilding plan would require a massive hike in annual costs in comparison to the average shipbuilding appropriations in recent years, according to a new report from the Congressional Budget Office.
Specifically, the Navy’s shipbuilding plan released in May would average out to an annual cost of roughly $53.8 billion — totaling a 41 percent increase from the roughly $38.1 billion the Navy has secured annually in appropriations during the last half decade, the CBO report released Thursday said.
This estimate factors in costs stemming from refueling nuclear-powered ships, and procuring non-battle force ships such as used sealift ships, among other things — costs that are not factored into the Navy’s 2027 shipbuilding plan, even though such expenses are typically derived from shipbuilding funding, CBO said. As a result, those factors increase the CBO’s estimate of the Navy’s average annual shipbuilding costs by roughly $4.6 billion in comparison to the Navy’s shipbuilding plan. Altogether, this marks an unprecedented level of spending for shipbuilding.
“The cost of the Navy’s 2027 shipbuilding plan is high not only compared with recent funding but also by historical standards,” the report said. “Over the past decade, funding for ship construction has reached its highest levels since the Reagan Administration’s defense buildup in the 1980s. Since 2016, lawmakers have generally appropriated an average of $2.5 billion more per year for shipbuilding than the President has requested, partly because of concerns that the fleet is too small to perform all its missions.”
Accounting for only purchasing new ships in the recent shipbuilding plan, CBO estimates those ships would rack up to $1.47 trillion in 2026 dollars over 30 years. That’s an increase from the Navy’s estimate of $1.23 trillion over 30 years, per the report. CBO attributed these differences in new ship construction estimates to differences in “assumptions about the design and capabilities of some future ships.” Additionally, CBO acknowledged that it employed different estimating methods and accounted for growth of labor and material costs differently than the Navy.
The Navy’s shipbuilding plan and budget request seeks a total of $65.8 billion for shipbuilding alone for FY27. To advance the Trump administration’s Golden Fleet initiative, it calls for expanding the Navy’s inventory to 450 ships, including battle force ships, auxiliary ships, and unmanned vessels, by 2031.
“The pace of shipbuilding would be fastest in the next 10 years, reflecting the service’s desire to increase the size of the fleet as quickly as feasible,” the CBO report said. “It would slow from the mid-2030s to the mid-2040s; then construction would ramp up again in the late 2040s and 2050s to replace smaller ships, with a service life of 20 to 25 years, purchased in the first decade of the plan.”
Meanwhile, the CBO report comes days after the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee proposed massively slashing the Navy’s shipbuilding budget, trimming roughly $18.5 billion from the Navy’s request. In total, Senate appropriators designated only $41.6 billion to shipbuilding in their proposed spending plan.

articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A cybersecurity incident that began Thursday was still ongoing Friday in the West Virginia Legislature. A spokesperson said the disruption did not spread to other government entities.
articles.full_text:
West Virginia Legislature hit with cyber incident affecting IT systems
West Virginia’s state legislature is responding to a cyberattack that has taken down its website and impacted IT systems.
Ann Ali, deputy chief of staff for the House of Delegates, told Recorded Future News that the attack started on Thursday and has continued through Friday.
“Upon discovery, the relevant teams immediately took steps to contain the incident and began an investigation with the help of outside cybersecurity specialists,” Ali said.
“In connection with the investigation, access to certain Legislature IT systems has been temporarily disabled. However, based on what we know so far, the incident appears to be limited to the Legislature’s computer systems.”
She added that no other state agencies or offices are impacted by the cyberattack. An investigation into the incident is ongoing but Ali did not respond to follow-up questions about whether it was a ransomware attack.
No hacking groups have taken credit as of Friday.
The West Virginia legislature is split between two bodies, a Senate and a House of Delegates with 134 total members representing the state’s 1.7 million residents. Multiple municipalities in the state have dealt with ransomware attacks in recent years, including the cities of Beckley and Westmoreland.
Security research firm Comparitech tracked 132 ransomware attacks on government bodies across the U.S. in the third quarter — a 91% increase compared to Q3 last year. At least 41 of the attacks involved U.S. based municipalities, including a major incident impacting Anne Arundel County in Maryland.
This week alone, residents of South Portland, Maine, lost access to critical city services due to a cyberattack, while Minnesota’s Otter Tail County notified its 61,000 residents of a data breach caused by a ransomware attack in July.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: US companies’ use of Chinese open weight AI draws rebuke from House chairmen
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: An investigation led by the House Homeland Security Committee focused on the dangers of U.S. companies using lower-cost open weight AI models for certain projects.
articles.full_text:
US companies’ use of Chinese open weight AI draws rebuke from House chairmen
A new congressional report focused on how some American companies are embedding China-developed open weight artificial intelligence models into their tech stacks calls the trend alarming and cautions U.S. firms against the practice.
Pointing to how Huawei and ZTE technology quickly found their place in the marketplace and threatened American networks, the new report warns that if China-developed open-weight models are allowed to take root, removing them down the road will take several years and cost taxpayers billions.
Open weight models’ numerical weights and biases are made public for download.
The joint investigative report — produced by the House Homeland Security Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party — focuses on Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor coding platform owner Anysphere as examples of companies deploying Chinese open weight models. The companies were using them for customer assistance, coding projects and taking inventory.
None of the firms immediately responded to a request for comment.
Report co-authors Reps. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) and John Moolenaar (R-NY) drew the 50-page-long report’s findings from hearings, classified briefings, and agency advisories. The lawmakers also received briefings from DoorDash, Airbnb and Anysphere about how they integrated China-developed open-weight models into their consumer platforms, enterprise software and other systems.
“The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay,” the report said. “While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap.”
Silicon Valley startups and Fortune 500 companies alike are adopting Chinese open-weight models because they are cheap, easily customized and work well, according to the report.
But those benefits come with significant negatives, the report said, citing federal investigators’ findings showing that Chinese developers “used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities.”
The report features 12 policy recommendations, including the imperative to build an American open-weight AI initiative, establish a standard for where models are sourced from, create an AI bill of materials, bar China-developed models from federal contract work and sensitive critical infrastructure functions and evaluate Chinese models systematically.
The report is important because it identifies and explains the risks posed by the U.S. not competing seriously in the low cost open-source model marketplace, according to Mark Montgomery, a cybersecurity expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
Because China is more limited in the frontier model space — dominated by U.S. firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI — its leaders have pursued a strategy to expand global dependence on their open-source AI, using the “traditional Chinese model of state policy and capital” to kill competition, he said.
“Companies and utilities, driven by bottom line resource decisions will, as always, ignore security and safety issues in pursuit of a lower front end cost,” he said. “China knows this recipe well.”
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The firm’s parent company, Neighborhood Intelligence, said in a statement that The Container Store has “restored its website and systems following a cybersecurity incident this past weekend.”
articles.full_text:
Container Store restores systems after cyberattack
The Container Store on Friday said it is recovering from a cyberattack that forced it to shut down its online ordering systems and limited in-store transaction processing.
The firm’s parent company, Neighborhood Intelligence, said in a statement that The Container Store has “restored its website and systems following a cybersecurity incident this past weekend.” Neighborhood Intelligence — a rebrand of Bed Bath & Beyond — purchased The Container Store in July for $150 million.
While the stores remained open throughout the week, they had to use “alternative transaction-processing procedures,” according to the statement. The Texas-founded company has about 100 stores across the U.S.
Neighborhood Intelligence said the incident only impacted The Container Store and did not affect its other brands including Bed Bath & Beyond, Overstock, buybuy BABY or Kirkland’s. Neighborhood Intelligence reported $509 million in revenue for the third quarter earlier this month, with the increases driven primarily by the acquisition of The Container Store.
The company said it hired cybersecurity experts to contain the incident and restore the affected systems. So far, it does not appear the hackers stole customer financial data, but did not address claims made by the cybercriminal group n0n, which listed the company on its leak site earlier this month.
The n0n cybercriminal group emerged in September, and cybersecurity experts say they specialize in ransomware and data extortion. The group has attacked more than 100 victim organizations and demanded hundreds of millions of dollars in ransoms.
The group initially forced victims to pay a 10% fee just to access its negotiation portal, but now forces companies to pay the full ransom before viewing any sample of the stolen information, according to SOCradar.
Allan Liska, a ransomware expert at Recorded Future, said the group launched its data leak site in late September and tried to recruit affiliates on a Russian cybercrime forum called RehubcomPro Forum in late October.
Liska said the group’s cybercriminal post claimed affiliates were instructed to only target companies that earn more than $10 million annually in revenue and were banned from attacking organizations in the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Record is an independent unit of Recorded Future.
Cybersecurity firm LevelBlue said the group has primarily targeted healthcare and pharmaceuticals but recently claimed to have troves of data from financial services companies and retail firms.
LevelBlue noted that the group has used an AI coding agent and paid AI services to write and debug its attack scripts, helping it scale operations quickly.
